groups.name: Biological approach
groups.intro: Nine content terms. Section A questions on these are labelled Biological approach.

groups.name: Cognitive approach
groups.intro: Eight content terms. Section A questions on these are labelled Cognitive approach.

groups.name: Sociocultural approach
groups.intro: Ten content terms. Section A questions on these are labelled Sociocultural approach.

groups.name: Research methodology
groups.intro: Not Section A content terms: Section A is never set on research methodology. You need these for Paper 2, the IA and, at HL, Paper 3.

terms.name: Animal research
terms.def: Studying non-human animals to understand behaviour, often because the procedure would be impossible or unethical with people. Findings have to be generalised to humans with care.
terms.flag: So far only short examples, such as Harlow's monkeys in HD-05. No card yet on how animal research is used.

terms.name: Biological reductionism
terms.def: Explaining a complex behaviour through a single biological level, such as one gene, one brain area or one neurotransmitter, while leaving out psychological and social factors.

terms.name: Brain imaging techniques
terms.def: Methods such as MRI, fMRI, PET and EEG that show the structure or the activity of the brain, so researchers can link brain regions or processes to behaviour.

terms.name: Chemical messengers
terms.def: Neurotransmitters and hormones that carry signals through the nervous system or the bloodstream and influence behaviour, such as dopamine, oxytocin and cortisol.

terms.name: Diathesis-stress model
terms.def: The idea that a disorder develops when a vulnerability (the diathesis, which can be genetic or psychological) meets enough stress from the environment.

terms.name: Genetic inheritance
terms.def: The passing of genes from parents to children, and how far differences in a behaviour can be linked to genetic differences. It is usually studied with twin, family and adoption studies.

terms.name: Localization of function
terms.def: The idea that particular areas of the brain are linked to particular functions, such as the hippocampus and forming new long-term memories.

terms.name: Neuroplasticity
terms.def: The brain's ability to change its structure and connections in response to experience, learning or injury.

terms.name: Neurotransmission
terms.def: How a signal passes from one neuron to the next across the synapse: neurotransmitters are released, bind to receptors and are then cleared away, for example by reuptake.

terms.name: Anchoring bias
terms.def: The tendency to rely too heavily on the first number or piece of information we meet (the anchor), and to adjust too little away from it.

terms.name: Classical conditioning
terms.def: Learning by association: a neutral stimulus that is paired again and again with an unconditioned stimulus comes to produce a similar response on its own.

terms.name: Cognitive load theory
terms.def: The idea that working memory has a limited capacity, so learning suffers when a task, or the way it is taught, overloads it.

terms.name: Cognitive models
terms.def: Simplified representations of a mental process, such as the multi-store model of memory, that break it into parts and make predictions that can be tested.

terms.name: Confirmation bias
terms.def: The tendency to look for, notice and remember information that supports what we already believe, and to overlook information that challenges it.

terms.name: Dual processing theory
terms.def: The idea that we think in two ways: fast, automatic and effortless (System 1), and slow, deliberate and effortful (System 2).

terms.name: Operant conditioning
terms.def: Learning from consequences: behaviour that is reinforced becomes more likely, and behaviour that is punished becomes less likely.

terms.name: Schema theory
terms.def: The idea that knowledge is organised into mental frameworks (schemas) built from experience, which guide what we notice, how we interpret it and what we remember.

terms.name: Cognitive dissonance
terms.def: The discomfort we feel when our beliefs and our behaviour do not match, which pushes us to change one of them or to justify the gap.

terms.name: Compliance techniques
terms.def: Strategies for getting people to agree to a request, such as foot-in-the-door and low-ball, which often work through commitment and the wish to be consistent.

terms.name: Conformity
terms.def: Changing behaviour or beliefs to match a group, either because we want to be right (informational influence) or because we want to be accepted (normative influence).

terms.name: Cultural dimensions
terms.def: Broad ways in which national cultures differ in their values, such as individualism versus collectivism and power distance, used to compare cultures.

terms.name: Emic approach
terms.def: Studying a culture from the inside, using ideas and methods that come from that culture itself.

terms.name: Enculturation
terms.def: The process by which a person learns the norms, values and practices of their own culture, mostly through everyday life rather than formal teaching.

terms.name: Etic approach
terms.def: Studying cultures from the outside, applying the same ideas and measures in every culture so that they can be compared.

terms.name: Models of acculturation
terms.def: Explanations of how people change, and what they keep, when they live in sustained contact with another culture, such as Berry's four strategies.

terms.name: Social identity theory
terms.def: The idea that part of how we see ourselves comes from the groups we belong to, which can lead us to favour our own group and compare it with others.

terms.name: Social learning theory
terms.def: The idea that we learn by observing other people, through attention, retention, reproduction and motivation, and that seeing a model rewarded makes copying more likely.

terms.name: Experiments
terms.def: The researcher changes an independent variable and measures its effect on a dependent variable. In a true experiment participants are randomly allocated to conditions; in a quasi-experiment they are not.

terms.name: Observations
terms.def: Watching and recording behaviour as it happens, described by setting (naturalistic or controlled), awareness (overt or covert) and the observer's role (participant or non-participant).

terms.name: Surveys and questionnaires
terms.def: A fixed set of written questions answered by many people, using closed, rating-scale and open items.

terms.name: Interviews and focus groups
terms.def: Asking people questions in person: structured, semi-structured, or as a focus group where participants also respond to each other.

terms.name: Correlational studies
terms.def: Measuring two or more co-variables as they already are, without changing either, to see whether and how strongly they are related.

terms.name: Case studies
terms.def: An in-depth study of one person, group or event, usually combining several methods, often because the case is unusual.

terms.name: Sampling techniques
terms.def: How participants are chosen from the target population: random, stratified, opportunity, self-selected or snowball sampling.

terms.name: Ethics
terms.def: The duties researchers have to participants, such as informed consent, the right to withdraw, protection from harm and debriefing, and the extra rules for class practicals and the IA.

terms.name: Reliability
terms.def: Whether a measure or a study gives consistent results, for example over time, between two observers or when the study is repeated.

terms.name: Validity
terms.def: Whether a study measures what it claims to measure and whether its conclusions are justified: internal, external, content, face and construct validity.

terms.name: Generalisability
terms.def: How far findings can be applied beyond the sample, setting and time of the study.

terms.name: Researcher and participant biases
terms.def: Ways the researcher's expectations or the participants' behaviour, such as demand characteristics and social desirability, can distort a study.

terms.name: Credibility, transferability and reflexivity
terms.def: How the quality of qualitative research is judged: whether findings reflect participants' experiences, whether they could apply elsewhere, and how the researcher may have shaped them.

terms.name: Descriptive statistics and graphs
terms.def: Summarising data with measures of central tendency and spread, and showing it in graphs such as bar graphs, histograms, box plots and scatterplots.

terms.name: Inferential statistics
terms.def: Tests that show whether a difference or relationship in a sample is likely to reflect a real pattern, with effect size showing how large it is. HL students read the results; they do not calculate them.

terms.name: Thematic analysis
terms.def: Analysing words, such as interview transcripts, by coding them and grouping the codes into themes that answer the research question.
